title: Named by deeds
hook: no one can tell all His names; the wise name Him by His works (Jaap 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, king of kings, lord of millions of Indras, and your line, above every throne. Today, the last two lines of that same first stanza, and a question: if the One has no mark, what do you call Him? Day three hundred thirty-five.

Every apartment building has them. The neighbors whose names you never learned. So you name them by what they do. The guy who waters the plants at six. The woman who always holds the elevator. The kid practicing trumpet, badly, with total commitment. You don't know who they are on paper. You know them by their deeds. And honestly, that might be the truer name. The first stanza of Jaap Sahib ends on exactly this idea. Today: named by deeds.
screen: `NEIGHBORS WHOSE NAMES YOU NEVER LEARNED.` → `THE ONE WHO HOLDS THE ELEVATOR.` → `KNOWN BY WHAT THEY DO.`

segments.voice: The first stanza of Jaap has stripped away every label: no mark, no caste, no form anyone can draw. It has called the One king of kings. Now it reaches its last two lines. First, the whole of creation speaks: gods, humans, demons, even the forests and the grass, and what they say is net net. Not this, not this. It's a very old phrase in Indian thought, used for a reality so large that every description has to be refused. Then the stanza asks the question it has been building to. Who can tell all Your names? Nobody. And then the answer: the wise speak Your karam naam. Karam means deeds, works, actions. Naam means name. Names drawn from what You do. That's the hinge of the whole hymn. Everything Jaap is about to say, salutation to the Merciful, salutation to the Protector, the Giver, the Destroyer of cruelty, these are deed-names. Not a passport. A list of what the One has been seen to do. Guru Arjan says something close in the Guru Granth Sahib, on page one thousand eighty-three: the tongue speaks names made from Your deeds, and Sat Naam, the true Name, is Your name from before all beginnings. So Sikhs hold two things together. There's a Name beyond all naming. And there are countless names that come from noticing: mercy here, protection there, a gift that arrived on time. The wise, Jaap says, don't argue about the first. They keep a record of the second.
screen: `NET NET: NOT THIS, NOT THIS.` · `WHO CAN TELL ALL YOUR NAMES?` · `KARAM NAAM: NAMES FROM DEEDS.` · `ANG 1083: DEED-NAMES AND SAT NAAM.` · then, large: `NAMED BY DEEDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one thing you've seen the Divine do, or, if that language doesn't fit you, one thing life has done for you that you didn't arrange. A recovery. A stranger's help. A morning that came after a terrible night. Give it a deed-name, like Jaap does: the one who sent help, the one who kept me. Hold that name quietly and breathe with it. If you pray, you can say it with Waheguru. If you don't, just let it be a thank-you. The bell holds the time.
Named by deeds. Karam naam: no one can tell all the One's names, so the wise name Him by His works.
Your line: named by deeds. Today, give someone a deed-name out loud: thank you, the one who always remembers. Let them hear what you've noticed. Day three hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Sikhs use many names for the Divine, Waheguru, Akal Purakh, Gobind, Kartar, and many of them, like Kartar (the Creator) and Dayal (the Merciful), are names drawn from what the One does.

myth: Jaap claims the wise know all of God's names
it asks who can tell all Your names, and answers: the wise speak the names drawn from Your deeds.
in the first stanza even the forests and grass say 'not this, not this'
all creation joins in refusing any final description.
the Guru Granth Sahib has a similar idea about names from deeds
Guru Arjan, Ang 1083: the tongue speaks deed-names; Sat Naam is the primal Name.

fork.setup: you want to name the One who has no mark and no form. what does the first stanza of Jaap say the wise do?
fork.reveal: karam naam barnat sumat: the wise describe Your deed-names. the rest of Jaap is exactly that, a long list of what the One does.

original.note: Gurmukhi: kirtam naam, names made from deeds, Guru Arjan's phrase on Ang 1083.

trapdoor: what you thought: God has a name, and that's it.
what it means: no one can tell all the One's names; the wise name Him by His deeds, and the rest of Jaap is those names.
what a scholar hears: 'net net' echoes the Upanishadic neti neti; 'karam naam' parallels Guru Arjan's kirtam naam set against Sat Naam (Ang 1083).

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1083 (Guru Arjan, Maru Solhe): kirtam naam and Sat Naam

notes: Closing lines of Jaap 1 paraphrased ('tribhavan maheep sur nar asur net net ban trin kahat / tav sarab naam kathai kavan karam naam barnat sumat'): confirm reading of 'karam naam' as names from deeds.
Guru Arjan, Ang 1083: 'kirtam naam kathe tere jihba, sat naam tera para poorbala' paraphrased; confirm Ang and attribution (Maru Solhe, Mahalla 5).
Neti neti cited to Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.3.6; confirm reference.
